Port Phillip Bay seawater temps

The temperatures shown here are sea surface temperatures derived from satellites. They are provided in several places, and what’s here comes from the European Union Copernicus service. This dataset (SST_GLO_SST_L4_NRT_OBSERVATIONS_010_001) has the global oceans divided into grids 0.05° x 0.05°, corresponding roughly to 5km x 5km. It provides “Foundation” temperature, which is the temperature of the uppermost layer of the ocean (typically at a depth of a few centimetres to several meters) that is not affected by diurnal warming or surface cooling due to solar radiation or wind mixing. It represents the baseline or background sea surface temperature from which the diurnal cycle grows each day.

The closest grid cell to Williamstown beach is centred on Lon. 144.875, Lat. -37.875. It’s a little bit offshore from the Jawbone, as the global data set excludes grid cells with a substantial proportion of land. As a result, the shallow water right on the coast isn’t included, and that water can get cooler or warmer than further offshore particularly on calm days. Two other snorkelling/diving spots are included; the SE corner of the bay (Blairgowrie, Rye, etc.) is 144.775, -38.375, and just outside Western Port (near Flinders pier) is 145.025, -38.475.

The temperatures are daily measurements, so the graphs are a bit noisy; some other places, such as baywinds, show temperatures averaged over a few days to smooth things out a bit.

Current year, with last year for an immediate comparison

Multi-year plots

We can put this year into a broader perspective in a few ways. The first figure shows the current year, with other years from the past decade in the background, and the second includes the data since 2002.

We can look at the current temperatures against the mean across many years, giving a clearer picture of seasonal patterns, but losing the year-to-year variation.

The last way is to look at the temperature anomaly - how current temperatures compare to past years. We do that by calculating the difference between current temperatures and the long-term (since 2003) average. In this case the day-to-day temperatures jump around a bit, so the anomaly is calculated using the average temperature for the past 7 days. Above-average temperatures are in red, below-average in blue. The daily anomaly is a faint line in the background.

Three places of interest to divers and snorkellers

Open coast sites, such as Flinders, don’t get as warm or as cold as those near the top of Port Phillip Bay (Williamstown). Places near the entrance of the bay (Blairgowrie, Rye) are intermediate, but closer to open ocean conditions.
